newsitem.title: UK: Zeneca launches new migraine drug.
newsitem.headline: Zeneca launches new migraine drug.

text.p: Zeneca Group Plc launched a new migraine drug in Britain on Monday and said it could stop the pain and nausea of the debilitating headaches within an hour.

The drug, marketed under the name Zomig (zolmitriptan), is one of a new class of drugs known as 5-HT inhibitors, which help stop the dilation of blood vessels in the brain that can cause the excruciating pain of migraine.
It was approved for sale in Britain and Sweden last month.
Doctors believe both the blood vessels and the nerves are involved in migraine. A variety of things can trigger a migraine, from stress to particular foods such as cheese or red wine.
Changes start in the brainstem which activates the trigeminal nerve system, which scientists think is the "pain generator". Blood vessels in the skull dilate, raising pressure.
Levels of the neurotransmitter 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) fall during an attack. Neurotransmitters are chemicals that help carry messages between brain cells.
Zomig makes it easier for 5-HT to hook onto and affect brain cells. It prevents the release of other neurotransmitters that make the blood vessels dilate.

A study of more than 2,000 migraine sufferers showed Zomig prompted a response in 81 percent of victims within two hours. Half the volunteers said their pain was gone. Bigger studies have shown the drug works and is well-tolerated.

It can cause nausea and dizziness and people with high blood pressure or some kinds of heart disease should not take it. Zomig seems to be more potent that Glaxo-Wellcome's Imigran (sumatriptan), a similar drug. Zomig was originally developed by Glaxo but was licensed to Zeneca under an agreement Glaxo made with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) when it merged with British drugs firm Wellcome.
Some researchers say sumatriptan and similar drugs could also act against a newly discovered peptide that dilates blood vessels and which may be released when migraine sufferers clench their teeth.
Six percent of men and 14 to 18 percent of women in industrialised countries complain of migraine. The debilitating headaches are often accompanied by nausea and hallucinations.
Dozens of drugs, ranging from aspirin to beta-blockers, which lower blood pressure, are used to treat migraine. None has been found completely effective and many have unpleasant side-effects.
Glaxo-Wellcome's Naramig (naratriptan) was recently approved for use in Sweden and analysts expect a marketing battle over the two drugs.
Several other companies are working on drugs known as serotonin agonists, which help the action of serotonin, a neurotransmitter that can cause swelling in the brain.
All in Phase III clinical trials, these include Merck and Co's rizatriptan, Almirall's almotriptan, Pfizer's eletriptan, and Vanguard Medica's joint effort with SmithKline Beecham, VML251.
A recent study found nitric oxide, a common chemical in the body, could offer a target for drugs. Nitric oxide dilates blood vessels, regulating blood pressure.
